name: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections

clinicalPearls: Trichinellosis follows ingestion of meat (classically pork, but increasingly wild game such as bear and walrus) containing encysted Trichinella larvae; most infections are mild or asymptomatic, but heavy burdens can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1810).
Disease severity tracks larval burden: light infections (<10 larvae/g muscle) tend to be asymptomatic, whereas heavy infections (>50 larvae/g muscle) can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1811).

Clinical course is biphasic: an early enteric phase (diarrhea, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea) in the first weeks, followed in the second week by larval-migration symptoms (fever, periorbital/facial edema, eosinophilia) and then a myositis phase as larvae encyst (Harrison 22e p.1811).
Periorbital and facial edema with subconjunctival, retinal, and nail-bed (splinter) hemorrhages are characteristic of the migratory phase of trichinellosis (Harrison 22e p.1811).
Most deaths in trichinellosis result from myocarditis (with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure) and, less commonly, encephalitis or pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1811).
Muscle involvement preferentially affects the extraocular muscles, biceps, and the jaw, neck, lower back, and diaphragm muscles, with symptoms peaking around 3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1811).

Visceral larva migrans (most often Toxocara canis) chiefly affects preschool children who ingest soil contaminated with embryonated eggs, producing fever, hepatosplenomegaly, wheezing, and extraordinary eosinophilia that can approach 90% (Harrison 22e p.1812).

Ocular larva migrans typically occurs in older children/young adults without pica and usually lacks eosinophilia or visceral signs; the retinal granuloma can mimic retinoblastoma and lead to unnecessary enucleation if misdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.1812).

Cutaneous larva migrans ('creeping eruption'), usually from the dog/cat hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense, produces an intensely pruritic serpiginous track that advances several centimeters per day; the larvae cannot mature in humans and self-resolve over weeks to a couple of months (Harrison 22e p.1812).

Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) is the most common cause of human eosinophilic meningitis; CSF shows elevated opening pressure, pleocytosis (150-2000 cells/uL) with eosinophilic pleocytosis >20%, elevated protein, and normal glucose (Harrison 22e p.1813).

Gnathostomiasis is acquired from raw fish/poultry (e.g., som fak, sashimi) and causes migratory, recurrent pruritic cutaneous swellings; CNS invasion produces eosinophilic myeloencephalitis with agonizing radicular pain followed by paraplegia, and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1813).
Stool examination is worthless in toxocariasis because the larvae never develop into egg-producing adults in the human host (Harrison 22e p.1812).
harrison.pathophysiology: These are zoonotic tissue-dwelling nematode infections arising from incidental human exposure; symptoms derive largely from invasive larval stages that (except for Trichinella) do not mature in humans. In trichinellosis, ingested encysted larvae are freed by gastric acid and proteases, invade small-bowel mucosa, mature to adults, and after about one week females release newborn larvae that migrate via the circulation to striated muscle, where most species encyst by radically transforming muscle-cell architecture into a 'nurse cell'; host immune responses help expel adult intestinal worms but have little effect on muscle larvae. Migrating larvae provoke a marked local and systemic hypersensitivity reaction with eosinophilia. In visceral larva migrans, ingested Toxocara eggs hatch, penetrate the gut, and disseminate to liver, lungs, CNS, and other tissues, eliciting intense eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation. In cutaneous larva migrans, animal hookworm larvae penetrate skin and burrow along the dermal-epidermal junction. In angiostrongyliasis, ingested infective larvae migrate to the brain and die there, inciting eosinophilic inflammation, hemorrhage, necrosis, and granuloma formation. In gnathostomiasis, aberrant migration of a single larva into cutaneous, visceral, neural, or ocular tissue causes local inflammation, including ascending migration along nerve tracts producing myeloencephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1810-1813).
additionalDifferentials: Polymyositis / dermatomyositis (myalgia, weakness, elevated muscle enzymes) - note T. pseudospiralis can mimic a prolonged polymyositis-like illness
Periorbital edema from other causes (allergic, nephrotic, angioedema)
Eosinophilic meningitis from other parasites (see infectionMimics)
Retinoblastoma (mimicked by ocular toxocariasis retinal granuloma)
infectionMimics: Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis in endemic areas: gnathostomiasis, paragonimiasis, schistosomiasis, neurocysticercosis, and coccidioidomycosis
Pleurodynia (coxsackievirus B) and bacterial myositis as causes of myalgia overlapping with trichinellosis
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood eosinophilia (develops in >90% of symptomatic trichinellosis, may peak at >50% at 2-4 weeks)
Serum muscle enzymes including creatine phosphokinase (elevated in most symptomatic trichinellosis)
Trichinella parasite-specific serology (titer rise usually only after the third week of infection)
Muscle biopsy (>=1 g, near tendon insertions in symptomatic muscle) with fresh tissue compressed between glass slides and examined microscopically, since routine histology may miss larvae
ELISA for toxocaral antibodies (may be negative in ocular larva migrans); leukocytosis and hypergammaglobulinemia in visceral larva migrans; chest x-ray for transient pulmonary infiltrates

CSF examination for angiostrongyliasis (opening pressure, cell count, eosinophilic pleocytosis, protein, glucose); A. cantonensis PCR on CSF/tissue (available via CDC and Hawaii Dept of Public Health)
redFlags: Myocarditis with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure (leading cause of death in trichinellosis)
Dysphagia, dyspnea, or diaphragmatic muscle involvement
Severe neurologic, pneumonic, or myocardial involvement in visceral larva migrans (rare deaths)
Ascending radicular pain and paresthesias followed by paraplegia in gnathostomiasis (myeloencephalitis)
Cerebral involvement with focal hemorrhages in gnathostomiasis (often fatal)
Permanent neurologic sequelae from heavy CNS angiostrongyliasis
harrison.prognosis: Most lightly infected trichinellosis patients recover uneventfully, with symptoms peaking near 3 weeks and subsiding gradually over a prolonged convalescence; heavy infections can be life-threatening, with death usually due to myocarditis. Most visceral larva migrans infections are self-limited (rare deaths from severe organ involvement). Cutaneous larva migrans self-resolves over weeks to a couple of months as the larvae die. Cerebral angiostrongyliasis is usually self-limited with complete recovery, though heavy infections can leave permanent neurologic sequelae or cause death. Gnathostomiasis cutaneous swellings can recur intermittently over years; CNS gnathostomiasis is a serious complication and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1811-1813).
pitfalls: Most mild trichinellosis cases remain undiagnosed; a high index of suspicion and a careful dietary/exposure history are needed.

Trichinella serology is typically negative until after the third week, so a presumptive clinical diagnosis (fever, eosinophilia, periorbital edema, myalgia after a suspect meal) may be required early.
Stool examination is useless in toxocariasis because larvae do not mature into egg-producing adults in humans.
Ocular toxocariasis can be mistaken for retinoblastoma, risking unnecessary enucleation; it often lacks eosinophilia and visceral signs.
In angiostrongyliasis, A. cantonensis larvae are only rarely seen in CSF and serologic tests are unstandardized and may be negative at symptom onset.
Arctic T. nativa larvae in walrus or bear meat are relatively freeze-resistant and may remain viable despite freezing, so usual freezing prevention may fail.
Gnathostomiasis may present with ocular or CNS involvement without antecedent cutaneous swellings.
harrison.severityClassification: Trichinellosis severity correlates with muscle larval burden: light/asymptomatic infection <10 larvae per gram of muscle; heavy, potentially life-threatening infection >50 larvae per gram of muscle. Clinically graded as mild, moderate, and severe (severe = significant myositis/myocarditis) per Harrison's tissue nematode framework (Harrison 22e p.1811-1812).
management: For trichinellosis, give a benzimidazole anthelmintic (albendazole or mebendazole) early to eradicate intestinal adults; for symptomatic visceral or ocular Toxocara larva migrans use albendazole, and treat trichostrongyle-type infections with the same benzimidazole class
Use systemic corticosteroids to dampen the marked larval-migration hypersensitivity in severe trichinellosis (myocarditis, encephalitis) and in ocular or severe visceral larva migrans

In angiostrongyliasis-type eosinophilic meningitis, prioritise supportive care with analgesia, corticosteroids and repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture for headache relief, as anthelmintics are of uncertain benefit
Provide symptomatic care with antipyretics, analgesia and hydration, and correct anaemia or malnutrition in heavier intestinal infections
Monitor for cardiac, neurological, respiratory and ocular complications, following eosinophilia and muscle enzymes, and escalate to critical care for organ-threatening disease
Refer to infectious diseases or tropical medicine, engaging cardiology, neurology or ophthalmology according to the tissue involved
Advise prevention through thorough cooking or freezing of meat, avoidance of raw snails, slugs and contaminated produce, hand hygiene and deworming of pets to interrupt zoonotic transmission
